newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: REITH ATTACKS UNIONS OVER OLYMPIC BUILDING
Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says the New South Wales government seems powerless or unprepared to take on the unions in the lead up to the 2000 Olympics.
Mr Reith says wage rises sought by building unions are inflationary and will cost jobs.
He says the state Government is letting the unions hold taxpayers to ransom over Olympic construction projects.
But the Construction Union says major construction companies are accepting union wage claims in enterprise negotiations.
WORRIES ABOUT MINISTER'S ROLE IN OLYMPIC APPOINTMENTS
New South Wales Opposition spokesman on the Olympics, Ian Armstrong, says Michael Knight's involvement in filling vacancies in the Olympic Organisation opens the opportunity for cronyism.
Mr Knight, who chairs the Olympics Organising Committee and is Olympics Minister, has taken responsibility for filling up to eight vacant senior executive positions.
Mr Armstrong says this could allow Mr Knight to put some of his political mates in the jobs.
He also says having the chairman doing the day-to-day mechanics puts a whole new management strata in place.
Mr Knight says the vacancies were always going to be advertised at the end of the year.
SMALL BUSINESS DELIVERS GLOOMY ASSESSMENT

Small business is downbeat about the state of the Australian economy but says things are looking up for next year. In the latest quarterly survey conducted for the Yellow Pages, 62 percent of of the 1200 small businesses questioned thought the economy had stalled.
Eighteen per cent considered it to be in recession.
But 46-per cent anticipated improved conditions in 12 months with only 11-per cent expecting things to get worse.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the Government's Budget forecast would be met, when Monday's business investment figures were stronger than expected.
But Economic advisor to the Yellow Pages survey, John Marsden, says today's survey results show the bulk of investment is confined to mining, telecommunications and infrastructure.
CAMPAIGN TO PROTECT OUTWORKERS HITS A SNAG
Australian retailers and the Textile, Clothing and Footwear Union are at loggerheads over the union's campaign to reduce the exploitation of outworkers in the clothing industry.
The union's angry because the Australian Retailers' Association has refused to provide it with a list of clothing manufacturers, and the retailers they supply.
The ARA says it is prepared to give the union a list of manufacturers, but the union says it can just as easily get such information from the Yellow Pages.
The association says meeting the union's demands would affect retailers' commercial confidentiality.
DEMAND DROP OFF A WORRY FOR PEANUT GROWERS
A peanut grower in Queensland's South Burnett says consumers will benefit from more stringent health standards now in place after a salmonella outbreak in peanut butter earlier this year.
The outbreak was traced to the Peanut Company of Australia's Kingaroy plant, causing some products to be withdrawn.
But there is some concern among growers about a drop-off in demand, as products withdrawn due to the outbreak are about to be returned to the shelves.
Grower, Peter McIntosh, says hygiene has been upgraded at all plants, and the health department is watching the industry closely.
Mr McIntosh says he's certain the peanut butter which goes back on sale shortly will be a top grade product.
STRIKE AT CHANNEL SEVEN
The media union says tomorrow's telecast of the Greg Norman Golf Classic is likely to be disrupted by a strike at Channel Seven.
Staff at the network have voted to strike indefinately over the targeting of nearly 120 jobs around the country and management's withdrawal of an improved redundancy offer.
The strike affects Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane and Adelaide, with Perth staff meeting this afternoon.
Dave Lane of the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance says there'll be severe disruption to news and current affairs programs tonight, at the very least.
The dispute is due to go before the Industrial Relations Commission in Sydney this afternoon.
CALL TO HONOUR INSURANCE AT COFFS HARBOUR
There's a warning that business people at Coffs Harbour will close up and walk away if they're denied insurance payouts for damage from last weekend's storms.
It comes from Coffs Harbour MP, Andrew Fraser, who says insurance companies seem to be considering rejecting a number of claims on the basis damage was caused by flooding rather than by rain water.
Mr Fraser says stormwater drains backed up because of high tides and it's most unreasonable of insurance companies to try to avoid paying compensation.
He says they also have an obligation to householders because some have been left with only a soggy bed and lounge suite, everything else having floated into the Pacific Ocean.
EXPANSION OF BOTANY BAY
New South Wales Ports Minister Carl Scully has announced a 100-million dollar expansion program at Port Botany which he says will provide a big boost to trade capacity and productivity at the port.
Patrick Stevedores will invest 100-million dollars to increase its terminal space at Port Botany and have its lease extended for a further ten years from 2008 by the Sydney Ports Authority.
The agreement includes productivity provisions requiring Patrick Stevedores to pursue operating standards comparable to similar international facilities.
DOWNER HAILS RELATIONSHIP WITH MALAYSIA
Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer says a record number of visa applications this month by Malaysians wanting to visit Australia shows the relationship with Malaysia is in very good shape.
Malaysia's Prime Minister Mahatir Mohammed says just because the race issue wasn't raised directly in his recent talks with Prime Minister John Howard, doesn't mean he isn't thinking about it.
Critisim in Australia of Asian migrants and multiculturalism has sparked concern in Asia.
But Mr Downer says this month has seen the highest number of Australian visa applications by Malaysian tourists and students in Australia's history.
GREG NORMAN PREPARES FOR BREAK
Golf... and Greg Norman says his upcoming three-month break is a sabbatical for his mind as well as his back.
As he prepares for tomorrow's Greg Norman Classic at Royal Melbourne, the world number one says probably 95 per cent of golfers have back problems.
Norman says the unnatural swing of golf is bound to catch up with you if you do it a lot.
But he says he's feeling fine for tomorrow's tournament.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
